title: TA9-23646
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXXXX XXXXX XXXX (principal claimant), XXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXXXX XXXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXXXX XXXXX XXXX, citizens of Colombia, claim to be in need of refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1
The principal claimant was appointed designated representative for his sons, XXXX XXXXXX XXXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXXX XXXX, who are minors.
The principal claimant is a 44-year old man originally from XXXX, XXXX, Colombia.

In 1998, he owned XXXX in XXXX in the XXXX area of XXXX, while living with his family in nearby XXXX. He was involved with the Communal Action Group (JAC) in XXXX. He said that in XXXX 1999, he received his first note from the XXXX of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) threatening him with trouble for interfering with FARC activities, which he believed had to do with his work with the JAC youth programs, which tried to counter youth recruitment in the area by the FARC. In XXXX 1999, a water diversion project of the JAC was dynamited by the FARC, who left notes asserting the FARC's control of the area. JAC sought help from the local police, who said there was nothing they could do. In XXXX 1999, he said he evaded a truck that appeared to be following him when he stopped beside a transport truck being loaded with bananas. When he later arrived at XXXX, XXXX gave him his second note from the FARC, which had been left by 2 men in a truck saying that he had evaded them this time but that he was in their sights, which he took to be from the FARC. A month later, he said the FARC left a third note on the body of a cow XXXX XXXX XXXX threatening him with death the next time. He reported this again to local police who said there was little they could do as this involved only the killing of XXXX and this area was a known "XXXX" XXXX of the FARC. Despite all these, he persisted with attending XXXX, until XXXX, 1999, when he was shot in XXXX while fleeing the presence of guerrillas XXXX. He had managed to reach a neighbouring XXXX where his neighbour drove him to a doctor in XXXX for treatment.

In XXXX 1999, while recovering from his wound at home in XXXX, his wife received a sufragio (condolence note) from the FARC offering condolences for his death. He also received a call from a colleague at JAC, a Father XXXX, that some FARC guerrillas who recently were caught by authorities had a list of targets, which included his name among other members of JAC.
As they already had U.S. visas they had applied for in 1998 for a vacation in the U.S., the principal claimant and his family left Colombia for the U.S. on XXXX, 1999.
The panel finds there is adequate state protection for the claimants in Colombia and they are, therefore, neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimants' identities were established by certified copies of their Colombian passports and other identification documents as tendered into evidence.2 State Protection

The determinative issue in this case is state protection, as to whether or not it was objectively unreasonable for the principal claimant to have sought state protection. As the other claimants in this case base their claims on his story, they are included in this determination.

While states are presumed to be capable of protecting their nationals, it was open to the principal claimant, according to the law, to rebut the presumption of protection with clear and convincing evidence that adequate protection would not reasonably be forthcoming to him and his co-claimants. I find, on the evidence, that he has not rebutted that presumption and, therefore, his and his co-claimants' claims fail. My reasons on this are as follows.

The principal claimant testified that between the JAC and him, they had filed reports with the police against the FARC threats but no investigation was initiated by the police because the police said they did not have enough to go on and the area was a "XXXX" or area with heavy FARC presence. On one occasion he was referred to the army but he said he did not seek help with the army as the nearest army station was too far away. He also admitted he did not try to seek the help of DAS (Department of Administrative Security) or GAULA (anti-terrorist unit on extortion and kidnapping) as he did not believe he would get any help from them.

When asked by the panel, he said he did not keep any of the notes he had received from the FARC, those he said he received at the farm in XXXX, XXXX, and XXXX 1999 and the sufragio received by his wife at their home in XXXX in XXXX 1999. This fact casts a serious shadow of doubt on the truthfulness of his assertions of having received such notes. Furthermore, while the FARC clearly had the opportunity to attack him or his family in XXXX, they had not contacted him there or at his regular 8-4 job with a XXXX XXXX firm. The FARC had not called him at home, cell phone or office or made any personal face-to-face contact with him or his family in XXXX. In evidence,3 is what he says is a note from the FARC which a nephew in XXXX, Colombia, was able to obtain and send to him just in time for his U.S. lawyer to file his U.S. asylum claim in XXXX 2006. Looking at the note, however, it appears to be one easily constructed by anyone with the aid of a computer, scanner or photocopier, aside from the fact it surfaced conveniently just so after the claimants' absence from Colombia of 7 years (1999-2006) just prior to filing his U.S. asylum claim, lending itself to grave doubt as to its authenticity. The panel, therefore, on the matter of these notes, does not, on a balance of probabilities, believe he or his wife received any of them or the one sent to him by his nephew is authentic.

As discussed herein, Colombia is a working democracy with the state apparatus to provide adequate protection to its citizens. The principal claimant's decision not to seek protection from the police or other state instruments is not reflective of the state's inability or unwillingness to provide adequate state protection to him and his family.

On the other hand, Canadian jurisprudence states the following: * States are presumed to be capable of protecting their citizens, except in situations where the state is in a state of complete breakdown. (Ward).4 * The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. (Ward).5 * The presumption of state protection applies equally to cases where the state (or an agent of state) is alleged to be a persecutor. (Hinzman).6 * To rebut the presumption of state protection, the burden is on the claimant to provide "clear and convincing" evidence of the state's inability to protect its citizens, (absent an admission by the national's state of its inability to protect that national). (Ward7). A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that the evidence establishes that state protection is inadequate (Flores Carrillo).8 The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate. (Flores Carrillo).9 * Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that the state's efforts are not always successful does not rebut the presumption of state protection. (Villafranca).10 * A claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state (Judge,11 Camacho).12 Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when one has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of a presumption of state protection. (Rio Ramirez).13

This paragraph is an attempt to summarize the current state of affairs on state protection and effectiveness of the state's efforts to provide her population with protection from terrorist groups such as the FARC and the ELN (National Liberation Army). The panel is respectfully cognizant of the various articles and reports submitted by the claimant in this respect.14 The findings in this paragraph and the next paragraph are supported by specific references to the documentary evidence addressed later in this analysis. The FARC has existed for more than 40 years, initially as a communist movement to protect the interests of Colombian peasants from the perceived excesses of the rich and powerful. Over the past decade and more, the FARC has become essentially a narco-terrorist group and appears to be devoid of its initial objectives i.e., to help the poor in the rural areas. In fact, these poor rural people are abused, targeted and victimized more and more by the FARC. The previous government of President Uribe was installed in August 2002 on the promise of serious commitments to fight and disarm the FARC. He delivered on these by dramatically increasing resources given to army and police and other state instruments. During his two terms in office, he did not manage to totally disarm and disable the FARC. The FARC still exists but its strength has been severely reduced due to persistent government efforts including substantial material help from Western powers, particularly the U.S.A. The FARC has shown some degree of resilience despite the setbacks of the past 8 years caused by persistent and escalating government efforts against it, but its capability of surviving these is currently the subject of much speculation dependent on how well it taps its new found focus on the drug trade vis a vis a determined government shored up by past and recent military successes, growing and almost total support by its population tired of the FARC-problem and heavy funding from the U.S. and other Western powers..

Documentary evidence, reflected in some articles and reports, does not always provide a precise picture of the current state of the FARC, mainly because there are too many interest groups painting somewhat conflicting pictures of the FARC, its strength and capabilities. However, objective evidence does question the current capacity of the FARC to harm civilians at will and to effectively communicate among its own leadership. Furthermore, most of the surviving leaders are hiding in deeply forested mountains along and outside the national boundaries. The state of Colombia has in fact gone beyond her national boundaries and apprehended or killed FARC leaders and destroyed their camps in adjoining countries, even creating diplomatic tiffs with Ecuador and Venezuela. Documentary evidence shows that the FARC still targets high-profile politicians, major human rights defenders and senior members of the army, police and judiciary in certain parts of the country. In November last year, they took credit for kidnapping a Governor of a department and killing him. Documentary evidence does not, however, support the point that the FARC is targeting people for petty extortion and or keeping track of them all over this vast country.

The current government of President Santos, which was elected on the promise of continuing the assault on the FARC, is going at it with renewed vigor and achieving success in demolishing the FARC leadership and structures. Colombia a democratic state

Documentary evidence15 that the panel views, on a balance of probabilities, as reliable clearly shows that Colombia is a functioning democracy where civilians have recourse to the state apparatus, i.e., security forces and police, when they require protection from criminal acts and human rights abuses and persecution. Those accused of such acts are held accountable for their actions through the rule of law. Elections were generally considered fair and free and took place in an atmosphere of freedom, transparency and normalcy.16 Moreover, a. Civilian authorities generally maintained control of multi-level security forces consisting of local, national police forces and a national army.17 b. The National Police are responsible for internal law enforcement, shared with the Department of Administrative Security (DAS) and the Prosecutor General's Corps of Technical Investigators (CTI).18 Europa World Year Book 200919

Furthermore, * Uribe resolved and delivered resources "...to strenghten the capacity of the government to achieve a lasting victory over the rebel groups. ...Issued a decree establishng a 'state of internal disturbance' and introducing a war tax... extended police powers, ...pledged to double the size of the army ...recruit a further 100,000 police officers". "In December 2003, the Congresso approved a series of antiterrorism measures, granting extensive powers to police and military" (p 1343). This also shows that the Uribe administration had in the past helped create paramilitary groups as an anti-FARC initiative, which was later found by the courts to be illegal, steering the government into resolving the problem by entering into a demobilization of these paramilitary groups in 2006. Several members of the Congresso and administration were prosecuted by the Supreme Court for involvement, thus showing a government determined at preserving the rule of law and upholding the independece of the Judiciary. * In April 2004, 17,000 troops were deployed in traditional FARC strongholds in a U.S. funded Military campaign (p 1344) * "... Colombian armed forces launced a raid on a FARC training camp in Ecuador, killing 17 rebels, including the group's second-in-command.." FARC was further debilitated later in that month by the death... of its commander-in-chief.... (p 1344) * The governemt secured a major victory when special forces rescued the group's highest-profile hostage (p 1344). US DOS Report20

Furthermore, * Guerilla group members continue to demobilize. In 2009, 2,481 guerilla groups demobilized compared with 3,420 in 2008. In addition indigenoeus groups are also leaving these groups and joining the reserves. * "FARC and ELN guerillas killed journalists, religious leaders, candidates for political office, local elected officials and ploticians, alleged paramilitary collaborators and members of government security forces." FARC-ELN alliances remained to be fragile - the FARC's 8,000 to 9,000 members and the ELN's 2,000 members worked together in some parts of the country and fought against each other in other parts. In 11 months of the year, the FARC killed 220 civilians. The FARC threatened and harassed doctors and nurses. * Political Parties operate without restrictions or outside interference. * Government officials have been forced to resign, were prosecuted and incarcerated for corruption and abuse of authority. The Supreme Court, with support and funding from the President, continues its investigation of Congreso members and senior government officials. Despite advances in the Justice and Peace Law process, the application of the law continues to face some problems. UNHCR Refugee Eligibility Guidelines21

Furthermore, * "Since 2003, President Alvaro Uribe committed to defeat the guerrillas pursuant to the 'Democratic Security and Defence Policy'. The current military efforts, such as the killing of FARC's chief commanders and the dismantling of its military structure, have significantly weakened the FARC....The Colombian Government reports that in 2009, almost 2,700 guerrilla members were demobilized." (p 4). This highly respected source also lists 11 groups that are targeted by the FARC, similar to the target identified by the U.S. DOS earlier. Noteworthy is that there is no reference to the FARC targeting people for their failure to pay the demanded extortion. Amnesty International22

This report indicates that * There was a rise in killings of members of marginalized social groups and indigenous people," who typically live in remote regions of Colombia where the FARC is present. * The number of kidnappings fell to 213 in 2009 from 437 in 2008. Most kidnappings were attributed to criminal gangs rather than the FARC or ELN (p 110).

UNITED NATIONS HIGH COMMISSIONER FOR HUMAN RIGHTS23 * Para. 29. The FARC-EP continued indiscriminate attacks, seriously affecting the civilian population, such as the launching of explosives, which killed 3 individuals in Corinto (Cauca) in May 2008; acts of terrorism, such as the attacks on the Cali Palace of Justice (Valle del Cauca), which resulted in the death of 4 persons and wounding 26, in September 2008, and the one in the village of Ituango (Antioquia) in August 2008, in which 55 persons were injured and 7, including one child, died. * Para. 30. Increased planting of anti-personnel mines by guerrilla groups has caused a high number of civilian and military casualties, among them children. * Para. 57. Judicial processes constitute a positive step in the struggle against impunity and the strengthening of the rule of law, which needs to be preserved and shielded from any politicization. * Para. 63. Previous reports of the High Commissioner highlighted the need to guarantee the rights of all victims and the importance of placing them at the centre of relevant public debates. In 2008, the plight of victims and their rights gained momentum within the political and public agendas. Among the victims, women have faced the most obstacles and stigmatization..." * Para. 66. The judiciary has also paid special attention to the rights of victims. In various decisions, courts have, for example, confirmed the right of victims to participate in the "voluntary depositions" under the Justice and Peace Law. * Para. 67. Public accounts about the sufferings of those kidnapped by the FARC-EP and of families of victims of extrajudicial executions have generated a feeling of anti-FARC-EP solidarity across the Colombian society. The media has helped to create social awareness....

OPERATIONAL GUIDANCE NOTE, Colombia, UK Home Office24 * Para. 2.6 ...the Government's respect for human rights continued to improve in 2007. Government steps to improve the human rights and security situation in Colombia showed demonstrable results during the year and government statistics indicated that there were decreases in massacres (34 per cent) and kidnappings (29 per cent). * Para. 2.7. Some serious problems remain, however, and in 2007 there were reports that elements of the security forces continued to collaborate with paramilitary groups, who refused to demobilize, who were responsible for serious human rights abuses and who had degenerated into renegade criminal groups more intent on the drug trade. * Para. 2.8. The Justice and Peace Law (LJP) process has exposed corruption and paramilitary ties within the Government and the security forces. In 2007, President Uribe urged the Supreme Court to punish public officials found guilty and continued funding of the Supreme Court's Investigative Unit, which investigates members of Congress and senior government officials. During the year, investigations by the Supreme Court and Prosecutor General's Office of links between politicians and paramilitary groups implicated 52 congressmen, 11 governors, and 19 mayors; 18 congressmen, 14 mayors, and 2 governors were in jail at year's end. * Para 3.6.4. In 2007, the FARC and ELN reportedly continued to commit human rights abuses, including political killings; killings of off-duty members of the public security forces and local officials.... * Para. 3.6.5. Sufficiency of protection - The state authorities are willing to offer protection to such individuals, however their capacity to actually provide it is limited due to the Government's weak authority in some regions and inability to counter the influence in parts of the country of the FARC, ELN, and paramilitaries who refuse to demobilize. While the new illegal groups lack the organization, reach and military capacity of the former AUC (United Self Defense Forces of Colombia, paramilitaries), guerrilla organizations continue to operate nationwide and are well-resourced to dominate areas in which they see a particular interest. The state therefore cannot currently offer sufficient protection from these groups. (It should be noted that the inadequacy of protection refers to persons outlined in para 3.6.4 above and not ordinary victims of attempted extortion, and the report is dated 2008 and thus may represent data for the years prior).

International Crisis Group April 28, 200825 * Almost 6 years of intense security operations against the FARC by the administration of President Álvaro Uribe are beginning to produce tangible results. Government forces killed several important rebel field commanders in 2007 and 2 members of the central command in March 2008, including second-in-command Raúl Reyes, and have severely disrupted insurgent communications, prompting a loss of internal cohesion and decreasing illegal revenues (page 1). * The national political climate has reinforced the government's stance. On 4 February 2008, over 4 million people marched against the FARC. The rejection of the FARC by the general population has been recognized by all political forces. An important faction of the left-wing Polo Democratico Alternativo (PDA) party has denounced the FARC's inhumane practices and clearly distanced itself from the insurgency, which it does not recognize as a legitimate left-wing force (page 2). * Recent successful military strikes against the FARC leadership and other signs of rebel weakness have led government and security force officials to claim Colombia was nearing "the end of the end" of the FARC. The government states that it intends to continue and even increase the military pressure so as to force the FARC to the negotiating table. It also asserts a willingness to use the Justice and Peace Law as the legal framework for removing the FARC from the battlefield, which implies FARC leaders could expect to serve no more than 8 years in jail (page 7). * The FARC's once stable command structure is believed to be faltering. The death of Ríos at the hands of his own men is a clear reflection of the loss in internal cohesion. Moreover, security force sources say that the lack of internal communication due to military pressure and technical surveillance and the increasing demobilization of experienced mid-level commanders are also affecting the chain of command. As morale crumbles, government officials believe political and ideological fissures will widen within the FARC leadership, prompting power struggles which could lead the organization to slowly fracture or even implode (page 7). * According to security force sources, the FARC is also increasingly less operational. Government estimates show it going from more than 18,900 fighters in 2002 to between 9,000 and 11,000 in 2007, with only 10 of its 71 fronts and units regularly active (page 8)... There is reason to believe that the FARC is still capable to a degree of adapting and resisting, at least in the short to medium term (page 8).

The situation of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia26 * The only source consulted that identifies the purpose of the kidnappings claimed by FARC is the Columbian online weekly Cambio, which states in a 28 November 2007 article that no ransom was demanded in 4 out of 11 kidnappings attributed to FARC in 2006. Instead, the kidnappers wanted to use the victim's business or bank accounts to launder money. * FARC's presence is felt primarily in the coca plantation regions in southeast Colombia (France2.fr 13 Dec. 2007). According to Cambio, the rebel group has withdrawn to the areas along the borders with Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama and its best fighters defend the territories where FARC is traditionally present - Guaviare and Caquetá departments, the southern part of Meta department, and Putumayo and Nariño departments. * According to Juan Manuel Santos, Colombia's Minister of Defence, FARC currently lacks means of communication (BBC 1 Feb. 2008). The BBC reports that "their radio and satellite communications are being intercepted thanks to U.S. technology" and that the organization has been forced to resort to using couriers (BBC 1 Feb. 2008).

International Crisis Group 2009 Report27 * The successes of the government's security strategy have resulted in part from the modernization and growth of its security forces, aided by substantial international technical and financial support, in particular from the U.S. Perhaps even more important have been improvements in the quality and quantity of strategic intelligence, which have enabled precision air raids to kill important rebel commanders and disrupt command-and control structures. * Key units of the FARC have withdrawn to the jungle and mountains, and they now rely heavily on ambush attacks. * As with organized criminal groups, drug trafficking has gradually taken over the heart of the activities of the FARC and parts of the smaller ELN. * At the tactical level, structures have decentralized; however, some reports claim the Secretariat is capable of co-ordinating actions around the country. * However, even though FARC has replaced its leaders in its senior command, co-ordination between senior and mid-ranking commanders remains to be difficult. * After pushing FARC out of heavily populated areas and regaining control of road arteries, ... the secuity forces are focusing on attacking traditional FARC strongholds. * Areas where FARC is strong and active are noted - western Meta, Purumayo, high mountain ranges or tropical jungle. (None of these include large urban populations.) * Security forces fear FARC will attempt to win back status in urbans areas through terrorism. Police have seized caches of explosives in the outskirts and FARC commandos have been arrested when attempting to penetrate cities. The first two complete paragraphs of page 12 indicate FARC urban structures have been disrupted; however, insurgents remain active in Cali and Bueneventura. Now FARC works in independent cells as support networks have been progressivly weakened. In the early 2000's, urban fronts were driven out of cities like Bogota, Medellin, Cali and Cucuta. Security forces have made logistics vulnerable to interception and exert tight control via checkpoints on roads and rivers that lead from combat areas. * Extortion may have increased but is still under-reported. Individuals may be using FARC's name as a mean to extract extortion. * Drug revenues have dropped from one billion to 500-600 million per year. * Increasing FARC defections make it easier for the government to collect intelligence. Ex-fighters are interrogated at the defense ministry - "sucked dry of information,"a U.S. embassy official said - before being sent to the presidency's high counsellor for reinsertion (Alta Consejería para la Reinserción, ACR). Based on their information, interception and infiltration of units has increased dramatically. Demobilized combatants are also instrumental in encouraging former comrades to defect. Increasingly, defection of mid-ranking and senior commanders with over ten years in the FARC helps to convince those previously under their command to desert. * After pushing the FARC out of heavily populated areas and regaining control of road arteries and other strategic infrastructure, the security forces are focusing on attacking traditional FARC strongholds. * In urban areas, where three out of four Colombians live, FARC support has virtually vanished due to public opposition to the organization's preference of armed struggle over political action and the government's success in depicting it as the main security threat to Colombian society. * By contrast, the FARC reportedly continues to exert control over and carry out indoctrination of inhabitants of the remote areas of Chocó, Meta, Norte de Santander, Antioquia, Guajira and Santander departments, as well as the coffee belt region (Quindío, Caldas and Risaralda departments).

Political handbook of the World 201028 * Fueled by proceeds from its drug trade, FARC grew rapidly during the 1990s reaching approximately 18,000 members by the 2000s. * This report also shows that Colombia is a functioning democracy with a bi-cameral parliament and universal suffrage.

International Narcotics Control Strategy 2010 for Colombia29 * Records coca eradication in 2008 resulted in significant decline in cocaine production potential and coca cultivation. * Pure cocaine production dropped by 39 percent from 485 metric tons in 2007 to 295 metric tons in 2008 compared with 700 metric tons in 2001. It is noted that FARC's area of control are primarily coca producing remote forests and even these are under constant attack and eradication. * High-Value Targets (HVTs). Because of the FARC's prominent role in the drug trade, over 60 FARC leaders have been indicted since 2005 in the U.S. for conspiring to traffic cocaine into the U.S. After achieving a number of high-level and significant victories against the FARC in 2008, the government maintained pressure against the terrorist organization and succeeded in capturing or killing a number of high-level FARC commanders in 2009. Under "Operation Fuerte," Colombian forces killed the commander and captured the deputy commander of the FARC's "Antonio Narino" urban front. On May 30, Colombian police captured Adela Perez, a senior FARC leader who participated in the 1994 car bomb assassination of a Colombian general and a 2001 assassination attempt against Colombian President Alvaro Uribe. * The government's National Directorate for Dangerous Drugs (DNE) reported that Colombian security forces seized a total of 205.85 metric tons of cocaine and cocaine base, 191.6 metric tons of marijuana, 740 kilograms of heroin, over 1.35 million gallons and 3.54 million kilograms of precursor chemicals, while destroying 285 cocaine hydrochloride (HCL) labs and 2,795 coca base labs during 2009.

Kidnappings and Extortion30 * The key perpetrators of the kidnappings for extortion were, on the one hand, the FARC (62 cases) and the ELN (39 cases), and, on the other hand, small-scale criminals (91 cases) (ibid.). * The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) indicates that the kidnappings, with or without extortion, took place primarily in rural areas and that "businessmen and public figures are targets . . . [for] guerrillas and common criminals" (20 Nov. 2006).

Crime in Colombia31 * In Colombia's 6 largest cities, the most common crimes are theft without violence (73 percent) and armed robbery in the street (20 percent) (ibid., 6). According to the study in Bogotá. * In 2008, 45 percent of people who stated that they were the victim of a crime reported the crime, compared with only 17.6 percent in 2007 and 40 percent in 2006; * The police registered most of the complaints (87 percent), followed by the Office of the Attorney General (Fiscalía General de la Nación) (13 percent); * 39 percent of participants felt that the police are doing a good job.

Update on the FARC Situation Although, the recent International Crisis Group report of 29 June 201032 recognizes security problems the country is wrestling with, there are indications of overall significant gains in this regard, notably as follows: * Page 1 - The government's campaign against the FARC "has taken a heavy toll on Colombia's largest insurgent organization. The government is now working to consolidate security gains by expanding state presence in several of the formerly most conflict-ridden regions" and the FARC as an organization "has lost thousands of fighters due to deaths in combat, captures and desertions...." * Page 2 - The research indicates that "across Colombia (Bogota, Antioquia, Narino, Choco, Norte de Santander, Meta and Sucre departments)... in 2010 FARC's military capacity is strongly reduced and the organization is experiencing serious coordination and communication problems." It said further that "in 2010, the guerrilla organization is estimated to have around 8,000-10,000 combatants, organized in 61 fronts (frentes), of which only 30 are believed to be active...." * Page 3 - "High levels of desertion have weakened the FARC and lowered morale among its rank and file." "Particularly problematic for FARC has been the increasing loss, especially since 2008, of mid-ranking commanders with a long record in the organization." This loss is considered acute because these commanders "tend to be responsible for maintaining discipline and morale among the troops and establishing relationships with local populations." "FARC has been unable to capitalize on the string of unilateral and unconditional releases of mostly civilian hostages it has carried out since early 2008." "FARC's diminished capacity and capability is forcing it to avoid large scale confrontations with government forces...." * Page 4 - "As of April 2010, the police had confiscated 1,663 rifles" and "6,000 arms were confiscated in the previous two years." * Page 5 - "FARC has lost most of its support among the population." * Page 7 - "Uribe's military offensive has increasingly denied the insurgents sources of income, particularly from kidnappings for ransom" forcing the guerrillas to shift their attention to the drug trade, putting into spotlight the change in the character of the organization as a radical political force to that of a criminal gang. * Page 15 - The report concludes that while the FARC has not been completely defeated, it has been significantly weakened due to the government's military successes.

A very recent Globe and Mail article dated September 29, 2010,33 talks about the "coup de grace" the current Santos administration has dealt on the FARC with the recent killing by the military of Mono Jojoy, "the military strategist and top commander of the organization" and Commander Domingo Biojo, political leader of the FARC's 48th Front. These along with the 2008 deaths of FARC founder Manuel Marulanda and secretariat member Alape are looked upon as the end of the FARC as an effective rebel organization in Colombia. Intelligence data seized from the FARC camps and from defectors has made it possible to even locate FARC members hiding across the border in Venezuela. The treasure trove of data seized from the recent raid on Mono Jojoy's camp is expected to yield more information contributing to the demise of the FARC. The article states that "FARC is now unable to operate effectively within national borders. No terrorist guerrilla has ever won a war in exile." Country Condition Reports from Counsel

Counsel submitted 2 packages of country condition reports, which the panel has taken into consideration with particular emphasis on the IRB response report and the more current reports, as follows: * IRB Response to Information request COL 103286E (Feb. 23, 2010)34 - the report includes an opinion of a professor of XXX at XXXX University, who indicated that whether or not the FARC would continue to pursue a relocated individual "depends on the value of that individual to the FARC," which makes sense taking into account the much diminished manpower and resources of the FARC. A professor of XXXX of the XXXX University of Colombia even goes further stating that since Colombia has increased its capacity to protect threatened or vulnerable people, it is "likely impossible" for the FARC, ELN and former AUC to track and pursue their targets all over the country.35 The XXXX professor defined her perception of value targets as: "a member of the political elite, business class, academia, or professional class and was targeted by the FARC for extortion and coercion to cooperate and provide technical assistance,"36 none of which include the principal claimant or co-claimants in the case at hand. Further into this report, the FARC and its lesser cousin the ELN have overall suffered a severe weakening of their capacity and influence in just about every region of the country,37 a trend that appears to be continuing into the more current reports. Based on the description of his activities and work as stated in his Allegations, I do not find the principal claimant, on a balance of probabilities, to have the profile of a value of target to the FARC as described. * International Crisis Group, Oct. 13, 201038 - the report provided suggestions to further improve on former President Uribe's military approach, which "did produce important security gains" for Colombia, by implementing changes to advance institutional and structural reforms needed to address illegality and impunity. With the wide support current President Santos has, he was defense minister under Uribe, the country appears on track with his declaration of "democratic prosperity" under a new emphasis on social and economic development."39 * BBC News "FARC Likely to survive Mono Jojoy's death"40 - the report recognizes the government's military successes against the FARC and the shrunken influence the rebel group has on the country's map, but espouses caution with respect to whether or not the FARC has indeed been relegated to history. However, while the FARC presence is still undisputed, it is noteworthy they have been driven out of major urban centres and into only 1/5 of the country, mainly in the rural areas, mountains and outlying parts of the country. Further to that, the FARC appears to have shifted its character mainly from political subversives to a criminal group engaged in the criminal activity of drug-trafficking, which puts into question whether or not they are still engaged in political persecution. For the most part, it appears that its powerful military and political leadership has been largely decimated, and with it the capabilities and centralizing skills of its central command, if even remnants of this still exists. * Swiss report "Mono Joyjoy's death does not mark the end of the FARC but a significant evolutionary step toward what the organization is becoming: a disconnected grouping of similar organizations all focused on the drug trade"41 - the full title is telling in that it recognizes the breakdown of the FARC organization largely due to government military successes against it and targeted killings of its key leaders. It further recognizes the loss of FARC's essential central command structure and therefore fragmentation into disconnected criminal bands spread out over Colombia's vast territory and mainly in the rural and mountainous areas. While the BBC News report (above) estimated the FARC "may have between 8,000 and 10,000 fighters"42 this more recent Swiss report indicates the FARC lost 2,128 soldiers in 2009 due to desertion alone and from January to October 2010, 1,924 soldiers due to desertion, a total of 4,052 in just under 2 years. The desertion numbers are expected to grow with President Santos' continued military offensives. The report states that "Santos stands on solid footing when he claims that October 2010 is the beginning of the end of the FARC,"43 but cautiously predicts it to be a slow and steady decline for the fragmented group relegated to the rural, mountainous and border areas. Summation of this analysis on state protection

The foregoing analysis shows that the state is responding to the needs of individuals, it has resources and it has been and continues to be increasingly effective. It is definitely not perfect. Corruption and impunity have been issues but these are being addressed and supported at the highest levels and the independent judiciary is using and expanding powers to prosecute not only the parliamentarians but also senior civil servants.

The FARC has shown a degree of resilience and still manages to operate but its sphere of influence is getting smaller and the fragmented organization's manpower has been reduced and relegated to some remote rural and border mountain areas, and more so away from the major urban centres, i.e. Bogota. The defense forces have been achieving tangible results with significant backing by the U.S. and other western governments. Based on the foregoing, I find that the state of Colombia is able to provide adequate, if not perfect protection. The Canadian courts have stated that the test for a finding of state protection is whether that state protection is adequate.44 I find that the state of Colombia is able to provide adequate state protection to the principal claimant and his co-claimants.

Furthermore, with FARC's significantly diminished capacity, territory, fragmentation and destroyed central command, plus the 10 years they had been away from Colombia, I do not believe, on a balance of probabilities, the principal claimant and co-claimants to still be in FARC data banks of military targets.
Thus the claims of these claimants fail.

The Refugee Protection Division, therefore, determines that the claimants are neither Convention refugees within the meaning of section 96 of the IRPA nor persons in need of protection under subsection 97(1). Their claims are, therefore, rejected. (signed) W. Lim W.
